piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: Non-invasive physiotherapy interventions for autistic children and adolescents using the F-words Lens Tool: A scoping review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Aim To map non-invasive physiotherapy interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder, using the F-words Lens Tool to summarize the main components of these interventions. Method We searched PubMed, Web of Science, PEDro, Embase, the Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Scopus for studies published between 2001 and 2026 involving autistic children and adolescents. Intervention components were analysed using the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System and linked to the F-words through the F-words Lens Tool framework. The review was co-developed with patient and public involvement. Results Forty-eight studies were included. Most interventions were delivered by physiotherapists (71%), whereas 29% were interdisciplinary. Twenty-eight distinct interventions were identified, with ingredients covering five F-words domains: Functioning (e.g. structured and repetitive motor task practice; 67.96%); Fitness (e.g. aerobic and resistance exercises; 60.7%); Friends (e.g. group activities and facilitation of social interaction; 35.71%), Family (e.g. parent training and adaptation of routines; 20.8%); and Fun (e.g. meaningful and motivating activities; 14.3%). No components related to the Future domain were identified. Interpretation Interventions mainly focused on functioning and fitness, with limited attention to the Future domain. The F-words Lens Tool helped identify important gaps and support more comprehensive, person-centred approaches.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Change Detection Unfolds Within a Shared Low-Dimensional Brain-State Landscape
piezas.resumenOriginal: Detecting behaviorally relevant sensory changes requires the coordination of modality-specific sensory processing with shared attentional and control systems, yet how these processes are organized and evolve across large-scale brain networks remains unclear. Here, we investigated the connectivity architecture and temporal dynamics of auditory and visual target detection using fMRI acquired during matched oddball tasks. Cross-modal partial least-squares analysis revealed a low dimensional architecture comprising two dominant, modality-general dimensions and additional modality-biased components. The shared dimensions distinguished a sensory attention action configuration from a higher order associative and contextual configuration, whereas modality biased dimensions showed distinct organization involving frontoparietal and attentional networks. Projecting these connectivity patterns onto time-resolved BOLD activity revealed a common dominant latent space with graded regions of preferential occupancy across modalities. Overlap-adjusted event-related analyses further showed that auditory and visual targets were associated with a similar initial displacement along the first temporal latent dimension, followed by modality-dependent trajectories, particularly along the second dimension. This later divergence reflected different balances of regional contributions within a largely shared cortical architecture. By integrating dimensionality reduction of high dimensional functional connectivity with network and temporal analyses, our findings link the spatial organization of distributed cortical systems to their evolving responses, revealing how shared brain networks can support both common and modality-dependent aspects of sensory target detection.

piezas.titulo: Acute high-intensity interval exercise in spinal cord injury: psychological benefits alongside cognitive and neurobiological responses
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionAcute high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) can lead to improvements in executive functions, but less is known on if, and through what mechanisms, this applies after spinal cord injury (SCI). In this randomized within-subject crossover study, the effects of acute HIIE on working memory, cognitive task-related regional cerebral blood flow, blood biomarkers and psychological responses were investigated.MethodsSixteen adults with chronic SCI [mean age 43.3 ± 10.6 years; 12 men; 9 with paraplegia (T2–T12) and 7 with tetraplegia (C5–C8); > 1-year post-injury] completed a passive rest and a HIIE condition (20 min of double-poling ergometry at 80% of peak power output). Working memory (n-back task) performance was assessed pre- and post- intervention (planned: 10 min; actual post-intervention delay: 16.1 ± 4.4 min) with simultaneous measurement of hemodynamics using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) over the prefrontal cortex and transcranial doppler ultrasonography of the middle cerebral artery. Blood biomarkers (lactate, cortisol and BDNF isoforms) and psychological responses (affect, physical and mental fatigue) were assessed at multiple time points.ResultsLinear mixed models revealed no significant interaction effects between time and condition for most outcomes, but lactate increased post-HIIE and psychological responses improved following HIIE compared to Rest.DiscussionThe single supervised HIIE bout was well-tolerated in this screened SCI sample. It did not affect subsequent cognitive performance but was associated with transient improvements in affect (PANAS-SF) and mental fatigue. Adequately powered studies are needed to determine whether HIIE confers cognitive benefits in individuals with SCI and to clarify underlying mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.23508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

piezas.titulo: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.24943v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

destilado.texto: El número de tokens generados ya no indica directamente la complejidad temporal clásica. Los autores demuestran que la hipótesis de una relación monótona entre longitud de tokens y tiempo computacional falla, y proponen LLM Complexity como métrica que captura la dificultad real. Así, usar esa métrica permite diseñar currículos de entrenamiento que mejoran la precisión y reducen el consumo de tokens.

piezas.titulo: An innovative gamified gait biofeedback interface targeting propulsion: feasibility and preliminary effects
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundEnhancing the beneficial effects of gait rehabilitation is an important area of need as most persons with a history of stroke continue to experience gait deficits following discharge from rehabilitation. Incorporating gamification and real-time biofeedback into gait retraining may provide benefits by increasing engagement and salience during stepping practice to target specific gait parameters, maximizing therapeutic benefits on walking function. The objective of this study was to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of a novel, customized, gamified gait biofeedback interface specifically designed to enhance propulsion during gait training.MethodsA repeated-measures design was used to compare 3 speed-matched treadmill walking bouts (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT04013971): (1) walking without biofeedback (noBF); (2) walking while receiving simple, real-time audiovisual conventional biofeedback (cBF); and (3) walking while receiving gamified, real-time audiovisual biofeedback (gBF). Gait biomechanics, physiological intensity, and self-reports of task workload, user experience, and engagement were analyzed from 15 participants (9 able-bodied, 6 post-stroke).ResultsCompared to noBF, both gBF and cBF showed significantly greater increases in peak anterior ground reaction force, trailing limb angle, and ankle moment of the targeted leg during biofeedback exposure (Min 3), which were maintained during the immediate post-test without biofeedback (post), with moderate to large effect sizes. Compared to walking without biofeedback, both biofeedback conditions induced significantly greater physiological intensity (heart rate and rating of perceived exertion). NASA-Task Load Index results showed that gBF induced a higher workload than cBF for mental demand, temporal demand, performance, frustration, and effort. Also, gBF was rated higher in the novelty component of the User Experience Questionnaire.DiscussionThis preliminary study confirmed the feasibility and promise of real-time gamified gait biofeedback, suggesting that gBF can induce similar enhancements in gait biomechanics and physiological intensity as cBF, while promoting greater task load and mental demand during walking practice. This work lays foundations for future studies that further refine and customize the game design, as well as evaluate the effects of gBF in larger samples and greater training dosage.Clinical trial registrationhttps://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04013971?term=NCT04013971&rank=1#study-overview, identifier (NCT04013971).

piezas.titulo: Introducing in-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2
piezas.resumenOriginal: GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter ( eBPF ) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy . We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads. GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration , allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly. Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it. Why GKE Dataplane V2? GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities: Scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads . High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices. Network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking , while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging , live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics. The in-place migration workflow Instead of having to manually move workloads to a new cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide : 1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights , and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces. 2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI update command. To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME \\\r\n --location=LOCATION \\\r\n --enable-dataplane-v2'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe57748ce10>)])]> 3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization. In-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico. Get started In-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you plan your broader transition. To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started: Review cluster eligibility and migration phases in About migrating to GKE Dataplane V2 . Follow the instructions in Migrate VPC-native clusters to GKE Dataplane V2 . Read GKE Network Interface, from kubenet to eBPF/Cilium to DRANET for background on the evolution of GKE CNIs. Explore GKE networking dataplane for large agentic AI workloads to see how Dataplane V2 scales for large AI clusters.

piezas.titulo: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.25066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
piezas.resumenOriginal: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028. But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns . This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs. Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized , “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation. The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead Key • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision • Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development • Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress 1. Alan Turing 1936 Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI. REALITY CHECK Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm. 2. I. J. Good 1965 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” 3. Backpropagation 1986 Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks. 4. Vernor Vinge 1993 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess. 5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky 1990s–2000s Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively. 6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010s Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities. 7. The race to self-improving AI 2020s Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it. 8. Reality check 2020s François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain. YOU ARE HERE 2026 AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion? THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES 1. The Intelligence Explosion AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control. 2. Danger Without Superintelligence The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control. 3. A Useful AI Future Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation , an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science. An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine. Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI. Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here. Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts. We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper , “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle. We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress. A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out , rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming. At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists. Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design) Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow. To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers . Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.” These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision. Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate. In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind. I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence . The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions. Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives. The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them. The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world. This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence. What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

piezas.titulo: No Group Differences in Shoulder Joint Position Sense Between Male Baseball and Female Softball Athletes and Controls in Virtual Reality.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Vision and proprioception are the 2 primary senses integrated to plan and execute upper-limb movements. Virtual reality technology enables the investigation of population-level differences in vision-proprioception integration during a shoulder joint position sense test within a 3-dimensional environment by dissociating vision from proprioception through visual hand offsets. A total of 122 participants (collegiate baseball and softball players and age-, sex-, and throwing side-matched healthy controls) performed a shoulder joint position sense test under accurate and offset visual feedback conditions in virtual reality. Participants demonstrated significantly more negative joint repositioning constant error and larger absolute error under offset vision compared with accurate vision (P .05). The mean vision-proprioception reliance score across all groups was 0.9, with 0 to 1 as the theoretical bounds, indicating strong dominance of vision over proprioception. These findings suggest that when both vision and proprioception are available, individuals across populations exhibit comparable repositioning errors through vision dominant integration. Future studies should further examine proprioception-dominant or sport-specific tasks, such as baseball catching or hitting, to clarify population and limb-side differences in multisensory integration mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: Early electrical stimulation after spinal cord injury: the Neuromuscular Preparation and Neural Preservation Hypothesis
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neurological recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI) is uncertain and may evolve over months, while paralysis-related deterioration of muscle and surviving neural pathways can compromise the biological system required to express recovered motor control. Waiting for voluntary movement to return before providing meaningful neuromuscular activity may therefore allow the system needed for recovery to deteriorate. We propose the Neuromuscular Preparation and Neural Preservation Hypothesis, which argues that early electrical stimulation should prepare the neuromuscular system before the extent of neurological recovery becomes apparent. Electrically evoked contractions may preserve the structural and contractile capacity of paralysed muscles, while stimulation-generated afferent activity may maintain useful physiological responsiveness in surviving spinal sensorimotor circuits. Experimental evidence further suggests that activity-dependent circuit reorganisation and cellular responses may contribute to the proposed neural effects. The novelty of this hypothesis lies in integrating muscular preparation and neural preservation into a single temporal and functional framework: neurological recovery provides the command, surviving neural circuitry provides the route, and prepared muscle provides the effector. We predict that preserving these complementary capacities early may allow subsequently recovered descending motor control to be expressed as greater stimulation-independent voluntary function. Human studies support the muscular effects of electrical stimulation and demonstrate activity-dependent neural plasticity after SCI, whereas direct neural preservation and the long-term functional advantage of early stimulation remain unproven. Prospective studies comparing early and delayed intervention, with complementary muscular, neurophysiological, and voluntary functional assessments, are needed to test this hypothesis.
